messages.subject: Disperal distance and occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
So I guess I'll throw in the first question.

I am currently working with a dynamic occupancy model, similar to those in Kery and Schaub 2012 Chapter 13. The occupancy model accounts for both false positives (misclassifications) and false negatives. False positives are a major confounding factor for the population.  I am interested in calculating the probability of colonization (gamma, and possibly persistence, phi) as a function of the distance to other occupied sites. Herein lies the problem. Occupancy is a latent parameter, and is therefore unknown. I have come up with two potential solutions and I could use some help as to how appropriate/inappropriate each solution may be or whether there are alternatives. Ideally, I would like to estimate a probability of colonization based on the minimum distance to an adjacent occupied site. Getting this estimate is going to be somewhat important since there is management occurring that I don’t think we can fairly assess since many nearby sites have become unoccupied and may therefore be unable to be colonized.

Proposed solution 1. I could calculate the distance to each site (fixed point count locations) where unambiguous detections occurred the previous year between each point, resulting in “distance to nearest occupied point” between each year and include this as a covariate for gamma. However this will not appropriately incorporate detectability and adjusted occupancy, so is a little rough.

Proposed solution 2. I would like to use occupancy at t-1, the previous year, influence colonization between years. So I was thinking I model dispersal like this:

Gamma[i,t]<- Beta[0] + Beta[1] *   min(z[ , t-1] * distance matrix[ ,i])  ) + Beta[2] * management[i,t-1]

Where z is the Bernoulli distributed occupancy and “distance matrix” is matrix estimating the distance between all sites (i by i matrix). I was thinking that I might be able to use z to turn on the sites on the distance matrix that are occupied during the previous year, and turn off the unoccupied sites, thereby regressing the minimum distance to an occupied site for each year. I'm not as familiar with how JAGS works with arrays either, so would multiplying these arrays have the desired effect of turning certain points off that were unoccupied?

Do either of these seem reasonable, or is there another more effective solution? I worry that not accounting for dispersal distance may distort the effects of management.

Thanks in advance for any advice and I'm definitely open to alternatives.

Brian Rolek

Using R, JAGS, jagsUI, on Windows OS

Chris

Hi all,
I'll take the opportunity to ask a question as well. I am suffering from a problem of ever-extending posterior distributions of N in a spatial-capture recapture analysis where I try to estimate density with zero augmentation. The higher the M, the further to the right my posterior of N goes, without end in sight. To address the problem, I tried to use the approximation of the scale prior proposed in the Box 2 of Link (2013) Ecology 94(10): 2173-2179. I did this by changing just one line of code in a BUGS model taken from the scrbook library (bellow). My question is twofold:
1) Is it really this simple? Just changing this one line of code should do the job?
2) Does it not matter that the pdf of the beta with parameters 0.001 and 1 concentrates most of the density near 0? I am assuming that this is not a problem, but it still feels a little confusing because I am so accustomed to the constant prior.
Thank you,
Gonçalo

sink("modelfile.txt")
cat("model {

   # Priors
   sigma ~ dunif(0,50)
   p0 ~ dunif(0,1)
   alpha1 <- (1/(2*sigma*sigma) )
   #psi ~ dunif(0,1)
   psi ~ dbeta(0.001,1)                               ### <----   psi prior changed here
   for(i in 1:M){
      z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
      s[i,1] ~ dunif(Xl,Xu)
      s[i,2] ~ dunif(Yl,Yu)
   }

   # Likelihood
   for(i in 1:M){
      for(j in 1:ntraps){
         mu[i,j] <- z[i]*p[i,j]
         y[i,j] ~ dbin(mu[i,j],K[j])
         dd[i,j] <- pow(s[i,1] - traplocs[j,1],2)  +  pow(s[i,2] - traplocs[j,2],2)
         p[i,j]  <-  p0*exp( - alpha1*dd[i,j] )
         ncapsnew[i,j] ~ dbin(mu[i,j],K[j])
         err[i,j] <-  pow(pow(y[i,j],.5) - pow(K[j]*p[i,j],.5),2)
         errnew[i,j] <- pow(pow(ncapsnew[i,j],.5) - pow(K[j]*p[i,j],.5),2)
      }
   }
   # for computing a Bayesian p-value
   Xobs<-sum(err[,])
   Xnew<-sum(errnew[,])

   N<-sum(z[1:M])
   D<-N/area
}", fill = TRUE)
sink()

When you say your posterior keeps extending, are you talking about the tail of the distribution?  Or does most of the mass also move to the right?  The scale prior does not address the latter - for that you simply have to keep increasing M, or recognize that your data are inadequate for estimating detection probability.  As for your questions:

1) According to Bill's paper, yes.  If you take the snowshoe hare code from Box 2 and fit the different model versions, they behave as described.  I've done it.
2) Even though the density is concentrated near zero, the rest of the (0,1) parameter space has non-zero support.  The data should overwhelm the prior.

I'd love to hear about other experiences with this scale prior though.

Hi Gonçalo,

If the tail of the distribution of N "keeps extending to the right",  I don´t see much problem as long as the estimation converges.  You should try to analyze the chains output.
If the mode changes, then you would have to continue playing with M.  But most likely, you are in the former situation, if I understood correctly your description.

Using a dbeta(0.001,1) as prior places too much of the density near 0.  I expect that you would need a higher number of iterations, if the real psi is not close to zero. Therefore I would advise against it.
 I prefer dbeta(2,2) -- symmetric, dbeta(4,2) -- skewed to the right, dbeta(2,4) -- skewed to the left.

I hope this helps you.

Daniel

Hi all,

              I’m wrapping up a chapter of my dissertation on beaver demography and I stumbled with a couple of details that complicate a bit the modeling of my data.

I want to estimate beaver survival by age, but:

1)      I have both telemetry data ( recorded twice a month between October and May for 4 years) and mark resight data (recorded 2-3 times during repeated observations at the  beaver colonies between January and March of each year)

2)      Transmitters can only be fitted to juveniles and adults. However, as we were recapturing individuals every year, we fitted transmitters to kits that at time t+1 became juveniles. Likewise, when transmitters stopped working, we were using mark resight (because individuals fitted with transmitters also had the colored eartags we used for mark resight) to assess survival. This means we can have individuals for which we only have mark resight data, individuals for which we had mark resight data and we  later added telemetry, and individuals for which we had both sources of information but only had mark resight when transmitters stopped working.

I was considering  to convert my telemetry data to mark resight events (particularly since I don’t have recordings in the austral winter) with a detection probability of 1 and then estimate p in the usual way for the mark-resight data. I would build a multistate model (as Kery and Schaub 2012 described in chapter 9 ) with three states: radioed animals, non-radioed animals and dead (somewhat similar to what Kery and Schaub proposed under “estimation of movement between two sites”).

 Does this approach make sense? . Any feedback on this will be highly appreciated

Alejandro

Michael

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

these last days I've been doing what I often do: analysing simulated data sets. Specifically, I've been simulating a data set for a static occupancy model with 267 sites and 3 replicate surveys, with a couple of covariates in occupancy and detection. I also fitted one categorical covariate (hab, a factor with 3 levels) which does not have an inbuilt relationship with occupancy, but was picked by AIC as important in one simulation replicate by chance. Then, I compared the ML estimates from unmarked with Bayesian posterior means (and sd's) from JAGS with usual "vague" priors.

The really vexing thing is that I obtain quite different estimates from ML and Bayesian posterior inference and choosing different vague priors makes the Bayesian estimates change quite a bit. For instance, with one set of vague priors, I get these estimates (col 1-2 are MLEs, cols 3-4 are Bayesian estimates, and first 12 rows are for occupancy and last 3 rows for detection).

                   Estimate        SE  Post.mean   Post.sd

(Intercept)       0.8644003 0.3645124  0.9894014 0.4416282

elev             -0.9625339 0.6067099 -0.8717928 0.7252839

forest            1.1236287 0.5459076  1.3576133 0.6501192

habB             -0.5570901 0.5721802 -0.3558317 0.7042055

habC             -0.5167085 0.5624032 -0.2306627 0.7695561

forest:habB       2.0528777 1.0260894  2.4370036 1.2149884

wind             -2.9443091 0.2820748 -2.8930361 0.2812428

I tested my data simulation function in various ways and believe it is OK, and same with my BUGS (and also with unmarked) code. So I believe that these are correct results.

It may be true that (1) on the probability scale, the differences in the intercepts are perhaps not so great and (2) that relative to the estimation uncertainty (SE and post sd, respectively), the discrepancies in some slope estimates are perhaps not so remarkable either. Still, I have never before observed such relative strong differences between ML and Bayesian posterior means estimates and would be happy to hear any comments.
